title: The One With The Stoned Guy

jokes.text: Why does my cinnamon stick have an eraser?
jokes.setup: Rachel receives what she thinks is a hot cider with a cinnamon stick
jokes.punchline: The 'cinnamon stick' is actually a pencil — confirmed by the group's reaction ('Oh. Oh, heh. That's why.')
jokes.explanation: A sharp cold open gag. The question lands perfectly — it's specific and visual, and the punchline is entirely in the audience's imagination before the characters confirm it. Good economy and structure for an opener.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, this isn't a cinnamon stick... it's a pencil with an eraser!

jokes.text: Miss Tedlock, you're looking lovely today. May I say that is a very flattering sleeve length on you?
jokes.setup: Chandler's boss calls him in — he's clearly nervous about being in trouble
jokes.punchline: He responds with absurdly specific, desperate flattery ('sleeve length') to deflect
jokes.explanation: Very Chandler — the specificity of 'sleeve length' elevates what could be a generic brown-nosing joke into something character-specific. Shows his nervous deflection mechanism perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's a great sweater. The sleeve length is particularly flattering on you.

jokes.text: Oh, listen, if this is about those prank memos, I had nothing to do with them. Really, nothing at all. Really. Nothing.
jokes.setup: Chandler is told his boss wants to see him at end of day
jokes.punchline: He immediately incriminates himself by over-denying involvement in unmentioned prank memos
jokes.explanation: Classic comedic self-incrimination. The escalating 'Really. Nothing.' repetition is well-structured and very Chandler — his nervous verbosity is his defining trait and this is a good expression of it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I didn't do it! Whatever it is, I didn't do it! I swear! I have no idea what you're talking about! I'm completely innocent!

jokes.text: Hey, you guys. Chandler's coming, and he says he has this incredible news. So when he gets here, let's all act like, you know... [Chandler arrives] Hey. GROUP: Hey. Never mind. But it was gonna be really good.
jokes.setup: Joey builds anticipation for a big dramatic reaction prank as Chandler approaches
jokes.punchline: Chandler walks in too fast for Joey to execute — deflated instantly, but Joey assures us it 'was gonna be really good'
jokes.explanation: A nice anti-joke. The comedy is in the failed setup — Joey's confidence that it 'was gonna be really good' with zero evidence is a solid character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm gonna organize a surprise party for Monica's birthday. I'll get everyone together, decorate the apartment, bake a cake...

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know what? Never mind. That's too much work.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: But I totally would have thrown the best party ever.

jokes.text: I just don't want to be one of those guys that's in his office until 12:00 at night worrying about the WENUS.
jokes.setup: Chandler explains why he quit his promotion, using workplace jargon
jokes.punchline: The acronym 'WENUS' lands as a crude-sounding word in an otherwise earnest speech
jokes.explanation: A running gag anchor for the episode. 'WENUS' is a genuinely funny invented acronym that pays dividends later. The straight-faced delivery makes it work. Sets up the callback at episode's end.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Thank you, thank you. I appreciate it. But I have an announcement. I quit.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, I quit my job.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You just got promoted!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know. That's why I quit. I hated it there.

jokes.text: "The WENUS"? — Weekly estimated net usage system. It's a processing term. — Oh, that WENUS.
jokes.setup: Rachel questions what WENUS means; Chandler explains clinically
jokes.punchline: Joey's 'Oh, that WENUS' — delivered as if this fully clarifies everything, implying he's just playing along with the crude sound
jokes.explanation: Joey's response is perfectly calibrated — three words that simultaneously pretend to understand while clearly not caring about the actual meaning. Great character comedy in a very small package.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't want this job. I didn't go to high school so I could work in an office. I went to high school so I could get OUT of an office.

dialogue.speaker: Boss
dialogue.line: Well, you're gonna have to work somewhere.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know, but I don't want to work in an office where the acronym for my department is WENUS.

dialogue.speaker: Boss
dialogue.line: WENUS?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Weekly Estimated Net Usage Systems.

jokes.text: Yeah, I just don't have a lot of chefing experience. Unless it's an all-toast restaurant.
jokes.setup: Monica is suggested as head chef for Steve's restaurant; Chandler deflects by claiming he lacks cooking experience
jokes.punchline: The 'unless it's an all-toast restaurant' qualifier is a self-deprecating absurdist aside
jokes.explanation: Economy is the star here — the specificity of 'all-toast' elevates what could be a throwaway self-deprecation line. Very Chandler in its sardonic precision.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What is the WENUS?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The Weekly Estimated Net Usage Systems. It's a system we use to track our daily productivity. If we don't meet our WENUS by Friday, we're all in trouble.

jokes.text: Can you see my nipples through this shirt?
jokes.setup: Phoebe is mid-sentence about Chandler; Joey barges in with a completely unrelated question
jokes.punchline: The abrupt, oblivious non-sequitur about nipple visibility mid-serious conversation
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical Joey interruption. The timing and non-sequitur nature are what make it — he's completely indifferent to the emotional conversation happening. Pure character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: WENUS. It stands for Weekly Estimated Net Usage Systems.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, so you're saying the WENUS is down?

jokes.text: No, but don't worry. I'm sure they're still there.
jokes.setup: Joey asks if his nipples are visible through his shirt
jokes.punchline: Chandler reassures him they exist even if not visible — a deadpan, absurdly literal response
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. The response takes Joey's vanity concern completely literally and twists it into existential reassurance. Maximum economy (9 words), perfect Chandler deadpan, and the 'I'm sure they're still there' has genuine wit — it's absurdly logical. Strong contender for best line reading in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A chef? Me? I can barely make toast without setting off the smoke alarm.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Last time I tried to cook, Monica had to call the fire department. And she lives with a guy who sets things on fire for a living.

jokes.text: Well, I have an appointment to see Dr. Robert Pilman, career counselor-a-go-go. I added the 'a-go-go.'
jokes.setup: Friends ask where Chandler is going
jokes.punchline: He adds '-a-go-go' to the counselor's title, then immediately explains he made that part up — undermining his own joke
jokes.explanation: The self-undermining 'I added the a-go-go' is a signature Chandler move — he makes a joke and then immediately dissects it, which is both his charm and his neurosis.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I got the job! I'm going to be a head chef!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's great! So you'll be wearing one of those big puffy hats?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes, it's a chef's toque.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A toque? That's what they're calling it? I've been calling it a 'hat of dreams.'

jokes.text: Ah, the lesser known 'I Don't Have a Dream' speech.
jokes.setup: Chandler laments he doesn't have a dream, unlike everyone else
jokes.punchline: Framing it as a lesser-known companion piece to MLK's 'I Have a Dream' speech
jokes.explanation: Sharp cultural reference deployed with real wit — 'the lesser known' framing is the key that makes it land. It doesn't just name-drop MLK; it uses the construction 'lesser known' to turn Chandler's self-pity into something genuinely funny and quotable. One of the episode's best lines.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: The blunt, inappropriate nature of the question

jokes.text: Oh, I love my life. I love my life. Brian's Song.
jokes.setup: Chandler is spiraling about not having a dream
jokes.punchline: Rachel sarcastically declares love for her life and invokes 'Brian's Song' (a famously tear-jerking sad film) to underscore how depressing Chandler's situation is
jokes.explanation: Functional sarcasm that requires knowledge of the referenced film. Works as a beat but is a bit of an easy pop culture reach. The 'Brian's Song' name-drop does add specific flavor but feels slightly dated even for 1995.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Do you think they're too big?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, no. They're... they're perfect. They're all-natural, they're perky. I mean, what's not to like?

jokes.text: It's not too big, not too small. It's just right. — Was it formerly owned by a blond woman and some bears?
jokes.setup: Phoebe describes the restaurant space using 'just right' Goldilocks language
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately literalizes the fairy tale by asking about the blond woman and bears
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-constructed Goldilocks subversion. Joey taking the Goldilocks framing completely literally is perfect character comedy. Clean structure and good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Chandler Bing Bing-a-Ding-a-Ding-Bong!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, could you NOT call me that?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Why not? It's fun!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Because it's ridiculous. And honestly? I added the 'a-go-go' part myself. It just came out.

jokes.text: Because you can make yummy noises. — What are you gonna make? — Yummy noises.
jokes.setup: Monica says she wants Phoebe there to 'make yummy noises' as audience feedback; Rachel mishears and asks Monica what she's going to make
jokes.punchline: Phoebe answers 'Yummy noises' — not understanding Rachel was asking Monica about the food
jokes.explanation: A nimble cross-talk gag. Phoebe answering a question meant for Monica with the immediately preceding phrase is a well-timed misfire. The economy of three lines delivering the complete joke is commendable.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't have any direction in my life. I just wander around, making jokes, no real purpose.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's not true, you have—

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, no, not you, Ross. You're definitely not going anywhere.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? Why am I—I'm standing right here!

jokes.text: Oh, you should make that thing, you know, with the stuff. You know that thing with the stuff?
jokes.setup: Monica agonizes over what to cook for the audition dinner
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's enthusiastic but completely content-free suggestion — 'that thing with the stuff'
jokes.explanation: Very Phoebe — her earnest helpfulness combined with zero actual information. The repetition of 'you know' amplifies how empty the suggestion is while she remains fully confident.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I have a nightmare.

jokes.text: Uh, how about Tony's? If you can finish a 32-ounce steak, it's free. — Okay. Ahem. Hey, does anyone know a good place if you're not dating a puma?
jokes.setup: Ross asks for a good date restaurant
jokes.punchline: Joey's suggestion of a 32-oz steak challenge is clearly inappropriate for a date; Ross's 'not dating a puma' punchline confirms this absurdly
jokes.explanation: A two-beat joke that works well. Joey's cluelessness about what a 'date place' means is classic, and Ross's 'not dating a puma' punchline is a good unexpected escalation — specific animal choice matters here.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: The Notebook.

jokes.text: Okay. Ahem. Hey, does anyone know a good place if you're not dating a puma?
jokes.setup: Joey recommends a macho steakhouse for Ross's date
jokes.punchline: Ross dismisses it by asking for somewhere for non-puma-daters — a dry, polite rejection that conjures the image of who WOULD go there
jokes.explanation: Ross's 'puma' comeback is sharp and economical. 'Puma' is perfectly chosen — aggressive, carnivorous, implying a very specific type of woman. Good comeback energy and good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's just right.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What are you, Goldilocks?

jokes.text: [AS BUG LADY] I love you, Ross.
jokes.setup: Rachel mentions that the woman Ross is dating studies insects at the museum
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately does a creepy insect-woman impression, lovingly addressing Ross
jokes.explanation: A quick physical gag that gets a mild laugh. The impression itself is inferred from the '[as bug lady]' stage direction. Functional but not particularly clever — it's a fairly obvious riff on the setup.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What will Rachel make for dinner sounds?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'll make yummy noises.

jokes.text: Well, I just thought we'd go to dinner, then bring her back to my place and I'd introduce her to my monkey.
jokes.setup: Friends ask what Ross and Celia's date plans are, with suggestive anticipation
jokes.punchline: 'Introduce her to my monkey' — sounds like a double entendre but is entirely literal (Marcel the monkey)
jokes.explanation: Effective misdirection. The audience reads sexual subtext into 'my monkey' only for it to be completely literal. Ross's obliviousness to how this sounds is perfect character work.

jokes.text: And he's not speaking metaphorically.
jokes.setup: Ross says he'll introduce Celia to his monkey
jokes.punchline: Chandler breaks from the group to directly address the audience's (and the other characters') double-entendre interpretation
jokes.explanation: A perfectly executed one-liner that acknowledges the double-entendre reading without winking too hard. Chandler playing narrator/straight-man is efficient and the economy (six words) is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, there's this great steakhouse. They got these huge steaks, like the size of your head.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, that sounds great. My date is gonna love it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, are you sure? I mean, those steaks are really big.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? She's got a healthy appetite!

jokes.text: Aah! ROSS: Celia, don't worry. Celia, he's not gonna hurt you. Soothing tones, Celia, soothing tones.
jokes.setup: Ross predicted Marcel would 'seal the deal'; Celia meets Marcel
jokes.punchline: Celia immediately screams in terror; Ross's advice to himself to use 'soothing tones' while she panics is the comedic highlight
jokes.explanation: The payoff to Ross's monkey confidence. 'Soothing tones, Celia, soothing tones' — Ross narrating instructions to himself mid-chaos is genuinely funny and character-specific. Good callback to his misguided optimism.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I love Ross!

jokes.text: He's got his claws on my... — Yeah, all right.
jokes.setup: Marcel is clinging to Celia during the chaos
jokes.punchline: Celia's sentence is cut off at a suggestive moment; Ross's resigned 'Yeah, all right' implies he can see exactly where Marcel's claws are
jokes.explanation: A nice visual gag that plays entirely in suggestion. The truncated sentence plus Ross's weary resignation does a lot of work. The audience fills in the blank, which is always effective.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm going to introduce her to Marcel.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, you have an actual monkey?

jokes.text: It's creamier. — Yeah? Well, is that better? — I don't know. We're talking about whipped fish, Monica.
jokes.setup: Monica obsessively asks Rachel to compare two salmon mousses
jokes.punchline: Rachel's exasperated 'We're talking about whipped fish' — stepping back from Monica's intensity to note the absurdity of caring this much
jokes.explanation: Rachel's perspective cut-through works well. 'Whipped fish' is an inherently funny phrase and using it to deflate Monica's obsessiveness is good character contrast comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So I'm thinking about using a monkey as a wingman.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A monkey? Ross, that's the worst idea you've ever had.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, no. Women love animals. It's a proven fact.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: The only thing women love more than animals is NOT dating a guy with a monkey.

jokes.text: I'm just happy I'm keeping it down, you know?
jokes.setup: Rachel is being asked to distinguish between two salmon mousses
jokes.punchline: She lowers the bar entirely — her standard isn't 'better' or 'worse,' it's just 'still in my body'
jokes.explanation: A solid follow-up to the 'whipped fish' line. The escalating lowering of standards is funny — not exceptional but functional and well-timed as a grace note to the previous beat.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So what do you think of this salmon mousse?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's good, but it's not as good as the one you made last week.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I didn't make one last week.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Exactly.

jokes.text: "You're ideally suited for a career in data processing for a large multi-national corporation." — That's so great, because you already know how to do that.
jokes.setup: Chandler spent eight and a half hours taking career aptitude tests hoping for revelation
jokes.punchline: The tests confirm he's perfect for exactly the job he just quit; Rachel's cheerful 'that's so great' is devastating irony
jokes.explanation: The situational irony lands well. Rachel's earnest response ('That's so great') before she catches herself adds to the comedy — she's instinctively positive before realizing this is terrible news.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So I took that aptitude test, and you know what it says I should be?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A statistical analysis and data reconfiguration... whatever.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's what you do!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know! Could I *be* any more middle-management?

jokes.text: Don't I seem like somebody who should be doing something really cool? ...Something.
jokes.setup: Chandler asks rhetorically whether he seems like someone meant for something cool
jokes.punchline: He trails off, can't even articulate what 'something' would be — the ellipsis is the joke
jokes.explanation: The trailing 'Something.' is the best part — the deflation of his own pretension in a single word. Character-specific and relatable but not a remarkable joke in isolation.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, at least you don't have to worry about getting anyone pregnant.

jokes.text: Oh, hey, you can see your nipples through this shirt.
jokes.setup: The nipple visibility question was asked by Joey earlier in the episode
jokes.punchline: Rachel casually informs Joey mid-Chandler consolation — the answer to his earlier question arrives at the worst/most irrelevant moment
jokes.explanation: Good running gag payoff. The callback arrives during an emotionally sincere moment, which is exactly when you want it for maximum comedic contrast. The casualness of Rachel's delivery is key.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't know what I'm doing with my life. I have no direction, no purpose.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, at least you're not a paleontologist who got a nipple comment earlier.

jokes.text: Well, it is amusing.
jokes.setup: Monica explains the tiny appetizer is called an 'amuse-bouche' (French for 'amuse the mouth')
jokes.punchline: Chandler responds with a literal translation pun — 'Well, it is amusing' — delivered with total deadpan
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever wordplay moment. The pun works on two levels — literal translation and Chandler's sarcastic dismissal of the tiny food portion. Clean, economic, and character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's a French term for a small appetizer.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So it's amusing?

jokes.text: I see. And I've sort of been maintaining my amateur status so that I can waitress in the Olympics.
jokes.setup: Monica chose a 'professional waitress' over Rachel for her dinner party
jokes.punchline: Rachel's withering sarcasm about 'maintaining amateur status' for the Waitressing Olympics
jokes.explanation: Sharp, well-constructed sarcasm. The Olympics framing is unexpected and specific enough to elevate a standard 'offended employee' reaction. Shows Rachel's wit and wounded pride simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, what? A professional waitress? Monica, I've been waitressing!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I know, but this woman has experience. Real experience.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So what, that's like saying the Olympics don't count because I've been running around my apartment?

jokes.text: You know, I don't mean to brag, but I waited tables at Innsbruck in '76.
jokes.setup: Rachel's sarcastic Olympics waitressing bit
jokes.punchline: She escalates by inventing a specific résumé entry — 'Innsbruck in '76' — making her sarcasm more elaborate and absurdist
jokes.explanation: The escalation to a specific Olympic city and year makes this exceptional. 'Innsbruck in '76' is such a precise, absurd detail that it becomes its own comedic world. This is committed bit-writing — Rachel has built an entire fake athletic career in two sentences. One of the episode's strongest moments.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I mean, I could be in the Olympics of waitressing. I'd get the gold medal in spilling coffee on people and the silver in forgetting orders.

jokes.text: Amuse-bouche? [Rachel offers the tiny appetizer as a peace offering]
jokes.setup: Rachel and Monica have had a tense exchange about Rachel being passed over for waitressing
jokes.punchline: Rachel diffuses the tension by offering Monica the tiny amuse-bouche — a callback to the earlier joke about the comically small appetizer, now used as a comic olive branch
jokes.explanation: A sweet and efficient callback. One word — 'Amuse-bouche?' — does triple duty: defuses tension, references the earlier joke, and gets a laugh. Maximum economy in callback form.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: Talk dirty to me.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Um, okay. Your... your pelvis is very close to my pelvis.

jokes.text: No, no, no. Talk dirty.
jokes.setup: Ross offers to tell Celia a weird story from his day on the train — a completely innocent, conversational opener
jokes.punchline: Celia redirects immediately to dirty talk — the whiplash from wholesome to sexual is the joke
jokes.explanation: Effective setup for the extended dirty talk sequence. The abruptness works well. Economically perfect (four words) but not particularly clever beyond the contrast.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's not a big deal! I was just making an anatomical observation.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, you yelled it across the coffee shop.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I'm proud of my knowledge. And frankly, I'm proud to cuddle with someone who appreciates scientific accuracy.

jokes.text: Say something... hot. What? What? What? What? Vulva.
jokes.setup: Celia asks Ross to say something 'hot' in a romantic/sexual context
jokes.punchline: 'Vulva.' — Ross panics and blurts out an anatomical term, which is both accurate and completely unsexy
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and one of Friends' great early-season moments. The buildup through repeated 'What?' beats creates mounting pressure, then 'Vulva' arrives as the most medically correct and romantically catastrophic possible answer. It's perfect character work — Ross is a scientist/academic who retreats to clinical language under pressure. The word choice couldn't be better: not crude, not romantic, just clinical. High originality, exceptional character integration, maximum economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I love cuddling.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well, I'm up to 47.

jokes.text: "Vulva"? — All right, I panicked, all right? She took me by surprise.
jokes.setup: Ross attempts dirty talk for the first time; extended buildup of anticipation
jokes.punchline: His best effort under pressure is the clinical anatomical term 'vulva'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's standout joke. The entire buildup — multiple 'What?' exchanges, the pause, the anticipation — makes the punchline devastating. 'Vulva' is funny because it's both accurate and completely wrong for the context. The word itself is inherently clinical, making it the worst possible choice for seduction. 'I panicked' is the perfect deflation. This approaches 8+ territory easily: it's character-specific (only a paleontologist-nerd like Ross would land on a medical term), structurally pristine, and the line has become culturally memorable from the show.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, so like this: Hey baby, you ever had your uh, your belly button licked before?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm showing you how it's done, man! You gotta be all smooth and sexy. Like, 'Hey gorgeous, you know what I'm thinking about right now?'

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey, stop!

jokes.text: Whoa, you cuddled? How many times?
jokes.setup: Ross admits that despite the dirty talk failing, they 'ended up cuddling'
jokes.punchline: Joey reacts to cuddling with the same scandalized disbelief he'd give to something actually shocking — 'How many times?' implies cuddling is somehow the transgression
jokes.explanation: Brilliant character comedy. Joey's moral universe is inverted — cuddling is treated as more scandalous than sex. 'How many times?' lands perfectly because it implies he needs to assess the severity of the transgression. Extremely Joey-specific humor at its best.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, so when you're auditioning, you want to make a real connection with the casting director. Eye contact is key.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Even if I'm reading the line about my dead grandmother?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Especially then. That's when you need to connect the most.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, could you maybe just... not look at me? Because this is weird enough without you staring into my soul.

jokes.text: Look, I tell you what. Try something on me.
jokes.setup: Joey offers to let Ross practice dirty talk on him
jokes.punchline: The offer itself — Joey's complete lack of self-consciousness about this suggestion — is the joke
jokes.explanation: Setup for the cringe comedy sequence that follows. Joey's breezy confidence in offering himself as a practice partner is character-perfect — he has no reservations, which is itself the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm just going to say it. Monica's been asking me to be more... spontaneous in the bedroom.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, you gotta talk dirty! Women love that!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I don't know if I can do that, Joey. It feels so unnatural.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Come on! Just practice with me. I'll be Monica.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's... that's not going to help.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, just try it. Say something sexy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Um... your hair looks... nice?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No! No! You gotta be more aggressive! Come on, you're a paleontologist, use some big words!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: How is that supposed to help?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I don't know, just try it!

jokes.text: Please be kidding.
jokes.setup: Joey offers to let Ross practice dirty talk on him
jokes.punchline: Ross's pained, minimal response captures his complete horror at the suggestion
jokes.explanation: Three words, well-chosen. Ross's delivery of resigned horror is a straight-man beat that works without being particularly crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Oh my God, I'm so sorry! I didn't see anything!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Monica, wait—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, no, it's fine. I'm happy for you guys. I mean, it's about time.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? No, Monica, you don't understand—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm going to go. And I'm not going to tell anyone. Your secret is safe with me.

jokes.text: Oh, Ross. You get me so hot, I want your lips on me now.
jokes.setup: Joey demonstrates dirty talk to Ross as an example of what to say
jokes.punchline: Joey commits fully to demonstrating sexual talk directed at Ross — the discomfort of the content plus Joey's complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Joey's commitment to the demonstration without any self-awareness is the engine of this sequence. The cringe-comedy of two male friends doing this in a 1995 sitcom gets an audience reaction primarily from the discomfort.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I steal office supplies from work, but it's not the same at home. There's no thrill. At the office, I'm sneaking around, looking over my shoulder... At home, I'm just taking my own stuff. It's depressing.

jokes.text: Now tell me you want to caress my butt.
jokes.setup: Joey coaching Ross through dirty talk practice
jokes.punchline: Joey escalates his demands — now Ross must direct specific compliments at Joey's body
jokes.explanation: Part of the escalating discomfort sequence. Less surprising than Joey's initial offer — by this point the joke is in sustained cringe rather than surprise. Still works as escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I don't want a raise.

dialogue.speaker: Boss
dialogue.line: Twenty percent more?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Boss
dialogue.line: Thirty percent?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I appreciate it, but no.

dialogue.speaker: Boss
dialogue.line: Fifty percent more and a company car!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Look, I'm flattered, but I really need to leave this job.

dialogue.speaker: Boss
dialogue.line: Name your price.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: There is no price! Well, there's a price, but it's not money.

jokes.text: Okay, turn around. I just don't want you staring at me when I'm doing this.
jokes.setup: Ross reluctantly agrees to practice dirty talk on Joey
jokes.punchline: Ross can't even begin without making Joey turn away — his discomfort is so profound he needs that minimal privacy
jokes.explanation: A good character beat within the cringe sequence. The specificity of needing Joey to turn around — as if slightly more privacy changes anything about this situation — is Ross's neurotic overthinking expressed physically.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Look at this view! Isn't it amazing?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is that a couple having sex in that office across the street?

jokes.text: I want to take my tongue and... [long pause] And... [more pause] Say it! Run it all over your body... [longer pause] ...until you're trembling with... [extended pause]
jokes.setup: Ross attempts dirty talk to a turned-around Joey
jokes.punchline: Ross's attempt is agonizingly slow, punctuated by huge pauses, where Joey keeps urging 'Keep going' and 'Say it' — the extended discomfort IS the joke
jokes.explanation: The sustained cringe centerpiece of the dirty-talk subplot. The escalating pauses and Joey's urging 'Say it!' create mounting comedic tension. The structure is excellent — each pause is longer than the last, and the unfinished sentences keep the joke alive without resolving. The non-resolution into the next scene is the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hi, it's me. I'm just calling to see if there's anything you need me to do... No? OK, well, I'm just gonna go ahead and make myself a cup of coffee then. You don't need anything, right? No? OK, great. I'll talk to you later.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I just wanted to call my secretary.

jokes.text: It's okay. It's okay. I was always rooting for you two kids to get together.
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler walk in on Ross apparently practicing dirty talk with Joey
jokes.punchline: Chandler responds as if he's walked in on an actual romantic moment — playing it completely straight
jokes.explanation: Chandler's response is perfectly calibrated — he commits entirely to the pretense that this was a genuine romantic moment ('I was always rooting for you two kids') rather than explaining or questioning. The 'you two kids' phrasing is the ideal touch. Strong Chandler moment.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, like I have real plans? I'm free every night. I literally sit at home and practice my sighs.

jokes.text: Yeah, it's a lot less satisfying to steal pens from your own home, you know?
jokes.setup: Chandler is on the phone with his old boss, claiming he misses the job
jokes.punchline: The thing he actually misses is stealing office pens — a hilariously mundane and specific grievance
jokes.explanation: A strong observational-comic line. The specificity of 'steal pens from your own home' captures the petty, mundane reality of office life in a single sentence. Relatable and character-appropriate — Chandler finds tiny rebellions in corporate drudgery.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: He's totally baked, you guys. Like, completely blazed. He's so stoned, he's basically a rock. Totally zooted. He's higher than a giraffe's butt in a two-story building. The guy is absolutely reefer-ed up. He's so pot-ed, I think he forgot his own name.

jokes.text: And that's on top of the year-end bonus structure you mentioned earlier? — BOTH: Your dream. — No, Al. I'm not playing hardball here, this is not a negotiation. This is a rejection. No... No, no. No, no. No, stop saying numbers!
jokes.setup: Chandler tries to reject his old boss's job offer on principle
jokes.punchline: Each time he resolves to be principled, the escalating offer weakens him further — culminating in 'No, stop saying numbers!' which reveals he can't even hear the offer without being tempted
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best sustained comedy sequences. Each escalation — the bonus, the friends calling him out, more numbers — strips away Chandler's resolve layer by layer. 'No, stop saying numbers!' is the perfect punchline: it's funny, specific, and reveals character (his principles immediately dissolve for money). Excellent structure. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm like, totally baked, you know? We were just chillin' and gettin' blazed...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Dave's not here.

jokes.text: I'll see you Monday!
jokes.setup: Chandler has been vehemently insisting this is a firm rejection, not negotiation
jokes.punchline: He immediately capitulates — 'I'll see you Monday!' — making the entire principled speech irrelevant
jokes.explanation: Three words that demolish everything Chandler said in the previous two minutes. The cheerful finality of 'I'll see you Monday!' after 'THIS IS A REJECTION' is pitch-perfect comic irony. Economy score is 9 — five syllables doing maximum comedic work.

dialogue.speaker: Steve
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Monica, this is... *makes exaggerated face* ...this is the best thing I've ever tasted in my entire life!

jokes.text: Wow. It's huge. It's so much bigger than the cubicle. — Oh, this is a cube.
jokes.setup: Ross visits Chandler's new office and is amazed by the size
jokes.punchline: Chandler confirms it's just a cube (cubicle) — Ross was calling a cubicle 'huge'
jokes.explanation: Functional but not sharp. The joke about the lowered expectations of office space is observational but not especially crafted. Works as a beat but is fairly predictable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I made tartlets.

dialogue.speaker: Steve
dialogue.line: Tartlets? Tartlets. Tartlets!

dialogue.speaker: Steve
dialogue.line: Tart-lets.

jokes.text: You have a window! Yes, indeedy. — With a beautiful view of... — Oh, look. That guy's peeing.
jokes.setup: Ross is excited by Chandler's window — building anticipation for a nice view
jokes.punchline: The 'beautiful view' is of a man urinating in the alley below
jokes.explanation: A classic misdirection-visual gag. The setup (beautiful view anticipation) is well-constructed and the punchline is broadly funny — New York grime undercutting corporate aspiration. The 'Yes, indeedy' from Chandler before the reveal adds good comic timing.

dialogue.line: His poetic description of ordinary taco shells

jokes.text: Helen, could you come in here for a moment? [Helen enters] Thank you, Helen, that'll be all. Last time I do that. I promise.
jokes.setup: Chandler shows Ross the new power of having an assistant
jokes.punchline: He summons Helen solely to dismiss her immediately — the entire point was just to demonstrate he could do it
jokes.explanation: A gem of a moment. The power-trip of summoning an assistant for no reason, then immediately apologizing and promising never to do it again, is very Chandler — he gets the thrill but can't handle the guilt. 'Last time I do that. I promise.' is perfectly self-aware. Strong character comedy.

dialogue.line: Steve getting increasingly excited about junk food. His enthusiasm for the most basic food possible

jokes.text: Wendy bailed. I have no waitress.
jokes.setup: Monica specifically hired a 'professional waitress' over Rachel
jokes.punchline: The professional bails, creating exactly the situation Monica's snobbery was meant to prevent
jokes.explanation: The irony is obvious and slightly telegraphed. Works as plot mechanics more than comedy. The setup for the negotiation that follows is the more interesting part.

dialogue.speaker: Steve
dialogue.line: I'm gonna save you, gummy bears. I'm coming for you. Don't worry, I'll get you out of there before the milk turns you into a soggy mess.

jokes.text: That's too bad. Bye-bye. — Ten dollars an hour. — Nope. — Twelve dollars an hour. — Mon, I wish I could, but I've made plans to walk around.
jokes.setup: Monica desperately needs Rachel to waitress; Rachel plays the leverage perfectly
jokes.punchline: 'I've made plans to walk around' — Rachel's absurd non-plans, deployed perfectly as a bargaining chip
jokes.explanation: The escalating negotiation is well-structured, and 'plans to walk around' is the standout line — using a completely valueless activity as a bargaining chip. Shows Rachel's lazy confidence and Monica's desperation simultaneously.

jokes.text: You know, Rachel, when you ran out on your wedding, I was there for you. I put a roof over your head, and if that means nothing to you... — Twenty dollars an hour. — Done.
jokes.setup: Monica appeals to friendship and gratitude to get Rachel to waitress
jokes.punchline: The heartfelt guilt trip immediately transitions to '20 dollars an hour' — Monica abandons the emotional appeal mid-sentence for a financial one; Rachel immediately accepts
jokes.explanation: The construction is very good — Monica begins a genuine emotional appeal and then abandons it mid-sentence for commerce. The 'Done.' from Rachel (who held out through $10 and $12) is a perfect button. Shows both characters' pragmatism.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So I treated it like an academic literary work. I analyzed the text, examined the subtext, and approached it with scholarly rigor. The villagers were very impressed.

jokes.text: Twenty dollars an hour. Done.
jokes.setup: Monica has given an emotional speech about friendship to guilt Rachel into waitressing
jokes.punchline: Rachel cuts straight through the emotion to '20 dollars an hour. Done.' — her pragmatism deflates Monica's dramatic plea perfectly
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the negotiation scene. The abruptness of 'Twenty dollars an hour. Done.' after Monica's emotional speech reveals that Rachel was always just waiting for the right number. The joke is in Rachel's total emotional detachment. Maximum economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey, I'm working late on the WENUS.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: The what?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The WENUS. Weekly Estimated Net Usage Systems. It's what we use to track productivity.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So you're trying to boost your WENUS?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm trying to get a big WENUS, yeah.

jokes.text: In the cab on the way over, Steve blazed up a doobie.
jokes.setup: The dinner party begins; Steve the restaurant investor arrives seemingly fine
jokes.punchline: Phoebe casually reveals Steve got high in the cab on the way over — complete non-issue to her
jokes.explanation: The revelation is a good setup for the Steve-stoned plotline. 'Blazed up a doobie' from Phoebe — with her characteristic breezy indifference — works well. Sets up everything that follows.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Oh my God! Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Client
dialogue.line: What? What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I just realized I have a surprise party to go to tonight and I completely forgot!

jokes.text: Smoked a joint, you know? Lit a bone. Weed, hemp, ganja. Okay, okay, okay. I'm with you, Cheech. Okay.
jokes.setup: Monica doesn't immediately understand what Phoebe means by 'blazed up a doobie'
jokes.punchline: Phoebe cycles through slang — 'joint, bone, weed, hemp, ganja' — and Monica cuts her off with 'I'm with you, Cheech'
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's enthusiastic synonym list is funny, and Monica's 'Cheech' reference is a clean stop to the escalation. Functional comedy, nothing exceptional.

jokes.text: Is it dry in here?
jokes.setup: Steve has just been revealed to be stoned; Monica and Phoebe are reeling from this news
jokes.punchline: Steve's first line of dialogue is the most stereotypically stoned complaint possible — cottonmouth — delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: A perfect character introduction for Stoned Steve. Four words that confirm everything — maximum economy. The timing (arriving right as Monica is processing the news) is excellent.

jokes.text: Well, smack my ass and call me Judy.
jokes.setup: Monica serves rock shrimp ravioli with cilantro ponzu sauce; Steve tastes it
jokes.punchline: Steve's stoned expression of delight — 'Well, smack my ass and call me Judy' — is an absurd, unexpected idiom of enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: This is a top-tier joke in the episode. The absurdist expression of joy is inherently funny, but what makes it exceptional is the combination: Steve's stoned state + Monica's anxious perfectionism as audience + the complete non-sequitur of 'Judy.' The specificity of calling for a woman named Judy adds an extra layer of absurdist randomness. Highly quotable, unexpected, and perfectly delivered as a character moment.

jokes.text: "Tartlets"? Heh. "Tartlets." ...Word has lost all meaning.
jokes.setup: Monica tells Steve about the upcoming 'tartlets'
jokes.punchline: Steve gets mesmerized by the word 'tartlets,' repeating it until 'Word has lost all meaning' — a philosophically stoned observation
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. 'Word has lost all meaning' is a linguistic-philosophical observation that only makes sense in Steve's altered state, yet it's also genuinely insightful in a comedic way — staring at a word until it sounds alien is a real phenomenon (semantic satiation). The construction is perfect: the repetition of 'tartlets' earns the punchline, which then transcends mere stoner humor into something almost poetic. Highly quotable, rewatch-worthy, and completely original. This approaches the 8.5+ threshold for exceptional TV comedy.

jokes.text: Oh, cool. Taco shells. You know, these are... They are like a little corn envelope, you know?
jokes.setup: Steve has wandered into Monica's kitchen while she's preparing; he discovers taco shells
jokes.punchline: His stoned observation — 'a little corn envelope' — is technically accurate but completely useless as a description
jokes.explanation: The stoned-insight joke: a taco shell IS like a corn envelope. The observation is funny precisely because it's both accurate and completely unhelpful. Works as part of Steve's wandering curiosity sequence.

jokes.text: Hey. Sugar-O's. — Oh. Macaroni and cheese. We gotta make this.
jokes.setup: Steve is noshing through Monica's kitchen; Monica is trying to steer him back
jokes.punchline: Steve escalates from taco shells to Sugar-O cereal to insisting on making boxed mac and cheese, completely derailing Monica's gourmet plans
jokes.explanation: The escalating stoner munchies vs. Monica's gourmet dinner is a well-constructed conflict. 'We gotta make this' said about boxed mac and cheese at a gourmet audition dinner is good situational comedy.

jokes.text: Give me the Gummy Bears. — No. — Give me the bears. — Well, then you can't have any. — Give them to me. — This is not worth it. — Oh, oh! Bears overboard. They're drowning. — Hey, fellas. Grab onto a Sugar-O. Save yourselves.
jokes.setup: Rachel tries to keep Steve from eating more junk food; he wants the Gummy Bears
jokes.punchline: Steve drops the Gummy Bears into his Sugar-O cereal bowl and creates an elaborate drowning narrative — 'Grab onto a Sugar-O. Save yourselves.'
jokes.explanation: An escalating bit that peaks perfectly. The negotiation over Gummy Bears is funny, but the payoff — Steve narrating a drowning rescue scenario between candy and cereal — is genuinely inventive and shows how far his stoned mind has wandered. 'Save yourselves' is the perfect button. Strong physical comedy that exists primarily in the imagination.

jokes.text: I've waited seven years for an opportunity like this, and you can't even wait four and a half minutes for a stupid onion tartlet? [OVEN TIMER DINGS] Hey...
jokes.setup: Monica reaches her breaking point and kicks Steve out of the dinner
jokes.punchline: The oven timer goes off exactly as she finishes her speech — the tartlets are ready at the worst possible moment, immediately undercutting her righteous anger
jokes.explanation: Beautiful structural comedy — the oven timer is the universe mocking Monica's outrage. She just threw someone out for not waiting for the tartlets, and they arrive the instant he's gone. The 'Hey...' trailing off captures Monica's exasperation perfectly. Timing-dependent comedy that works brilliantly on the page and even better with the physical performance.

jokes.text: What a tool. You don't want to work for a guy like that.
jokes.setup: Monica is devastated after the failed dinner audition
jokes.punchline: Rachel's breezy, unapologetic 'What a tool' about the guy Monica had pinned her dreams on
jokes.explanation: Functional but generic. 'What a tool' is the laziest possible dismissal and doesn't show much craft. Works as a character beat (Rachel's bluntness) but the comedy is minimal.

jokes.text: Yeah, you know all those yummy noises? I wasn't faking.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is reassuring Monica that her food was genuinely delicious
jokes.punchline: 'I wasn't faking' — a sexual innuendo framing applied to food sounds, with the added implication that Phoebe normally does fake 'yummy noises' (or that the phrase sounds inappropriate)
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's cleverest callbacks. 'I wasn't faking' is a sexually charged phrase applied to food appreciation noises — Phoebe says it with total innocence, which makes the innuendo funnier. It also callbacks to the 'yummy noises' joke from the beginning, tying the episode's Monica subplot together neatly.

jokes.text: Yeah, you know all those yummy noises? I wasn't faking.
jokes.setup: The group is consoling Monica about the failed dinner audition
jokes.punchline: Phoebe assures Monica her cooking was genuinely good by invoking the classic 'I wasn't faking' line — borrowed from sexual performance and applied to food tasting
jokes.explanation: A very strong callback. 'I wasn't faking' borrows from the idiom of sexual performance and applies it to Phoebe's food reactions established at the top of the episode. The implication — that tasting food is analogous enough to sex that you might fake it — is a clever, slightly subversive joke. Perfect economy and a satisfying episode-long callback. One of the better punchlines in the half hour.

jokes.text: I was the James Michener of dirty talk. It was the most elaborate filth you have ever heard. There were characters, plot lines, themes, a motif. At one point, there were villagers.
jokes.setup: Ross reports back on how his date with Celia went after practicing dirty talk
jokes.punchline: His dirty talk apparently evolved into full narrative fiction — 'characters, plot lines, themes, a motif...villagers'
jokes.explanation: The episode's finest joke and a genuine standout by any metric. Ross — a paleontologist and classic overthinker — has transformed dirty talk into literary fiction with 'a motif.' The escalation to 'at one point, there were villagers' is the perfect button: it implies scope and world-building that is completely incompatible with sexy context. This is deeply character-specific (only Ross would reference James Michener and include a motif in dirty talk), brilliantly structured, and immediately quotable. 'At one point, there were villagers' alone is a 10/10 line. This is one of the best jokes in early Friends.

jokes.text: ...it was kind of late and we were both exhausted, so... — You cuddled. — Yeah, which was nice.
jokes.setup: After the epic dirty talk narrative, Ross trails off about how the evening ended
jokes.punchline: The group correctly predicts he cuddled again — confirming the running gag and that nothing changed
jokes.explanation: A satisfying running gag closer. The group beating Ross to the punchline ('You cuddled.') and Ross's fond 'Yeah, which was nice' is a good comedic button on the subplot. The predictability is intentional and earned.

jokes.text: Yes, Fran, I know what time it is, but I'm looking at the WENUS and I'm not happy. Oh, really? Well, let me tell you something. You will care about it because I care about it. Got it? Good!
jokes.setup: The group wonders where Chandler is; his friends go to find him
jokes.punchline: Chandler is on the phone at work at night, aggressively managing the WENUS — exactly the fate he said he was trying to avoid by quitting
jokes.explanation: The perfect closing irony for Chandler's entire episode arc. He quit to avoid being 'one of those guys in his office until midnight worrying about the WENUS' — and here he is, at night, worrying intensely about the WENUS. The callback is structurally impeccable: it closes a loop opened in the first act. 'You will care about it because I care about it' shows he's not just doing the job but has fully internalized the corporate obsession. Exceptional structural comedy and character work combined.

jokes.text: How's this? Eek! Sorry. How about over here? Oh! See, now, that just means it's working. Does this hurt? No. How about this? Aah! There you go. [massage sounds and screaming continue]
jokes.setup: The episode ends with Phoebe giving a massage
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's massage is apparently painful/alarming — the client screams repeatedly while Phoebe reassures them that screaming 'just means it's working' — her confident incompetence is the joke
jokes.explanation: 'See, now, that just means it's working' is Phoebe's confident reframe of what is clearly a terrible massage — her unshakeable belief in her own abilities despite the screaming client is perfectly in character. A functional tag-scene button, though not as strong as the Chandler WENUS callback.

tmdb_overview: Monica cooks a gourmet meal for a restaurateur looking for a new chef but, unfortunately, he's stoned. After working as a data processing permanent temp for five years, Chandler gets promoted. And Ross has a date with a beautiful colleague.
insight: Stoned landlord visit grounds the episode—solid character comedy rescues a below-average 67.8 score.
